title: Serpents and doves (Matthew 10:16–33)
hook: wise as serpents, harmless as doves; not a sparrow falls without your Father
tomorrow: how does a speech about a sword end with a cup of water?

segments.voice: That was a week on the road with Matthew: follow now, a storm, mercy at a table, two daughters, a big field, a free gift. Yesterday's line: freely give.

Some advice comes in two halves that seem to fight: be kind, but don't be a doormat. Jesus gives it to the twelve with animals, right after the packing list. "Behold, I send you forth as sheep in the midst of wolves: be ye therefore wise as serpents, and harmless as doves." They'll be brought before governors and kings, he warns, and when it happens, they're to "take no thought how or what ye shall speak." Not much of a recruiting pitch.
screen: `KIND, BUT NOT A DOORMAT.` → `SHEEP AMONG WOLVES.` → `SERPENTS AND DOVES.`

segments.voice: Two animals with opposite reputations in the Bible. Back in Genesis, "the serpent was more subtil than any beast of the field." The dove is the bird Noah sent from the ark, and at Jesus' baptism the Spirit came down like one. He doesn't ask the twelve to pick. He asks for both at once. Wise alone can slide into cunning. Harmless alone can walk straight into the wolves. Together: a person who sees the trap clearly and still won't set one. Then he turns from danger to small birds: "Are not two sparrows sold for a farthing? and one of them shall not fall on the ground without your Father. But the very hairs of your head are all numbered. Fear ye not therefore, ye are of more value than many sparrows." One to tell a friend tonight: two sparrows for one small coin, and still not one falls unnoticed. That's what lets sheep stay gentle among wolves. Not that the danger is small, but that they aren't alone in it.
screen: `SUBTIL AS THE SERPENT.` · `GENTLE AS THE DOVE.` · `BOTH AT ONCE.` · `NOT ONE SPARROW FALLS.` · then, large: `WISE AND HARMLESS.`

segments.voice: Listen for the smallest sound you can find: a bird outside, a tick in the wall, the hum of the fridge. Rest your attention there as if it mattered, the way Matthew says not one sparrow falls unnoticed.
Serpents and doves. Wise enough to see the trap, harmless enough never to set one.
Keep this one: wise and harmless, both at once, among sparrows that are counted. Another week, done.

howItsDone: Some Christians turn to wise as serpents, harmless as doves when facing hard dealings at work or in public life, and some pray Matthew 10:29–31 in times of fear.

original.note: Greek: wise, sensible, shrewd. the word in Matthew 10:16 for wise as serpents.

trapdoor: what you thought: serpents and doves is a riddle about animals.
what it means: Jesus asks the twelve to be clear-eyed and gentle at once, sheep sent among wolves who are not alone.
what a scholar hears: Genesis calls the serpent more subtil than any beast of the field, and the dove came down at Jesus' baptism; the line joins both, then turns to sparrows.
guess: being clear-eyed and gentle at the same time
a warning to keep away from snakes and birds
choosing cleverness over kindness when it counts
recall: Let the dead bury their dead

chat.says: party was good. Dale stayed an hour. Aunt Jo cornered me: "you set this up." what do i say?
options: Wise and harmless: own it plainly, "I did, for Pop," and skip the jab you want to add.
Deny it. Wise as serpents means staying slippery so nobody can pin it on you.
Apologize for all of it. Harmless as doves means never standing by what you did.
chat.meaning: Jesus asked for both at once: wise as serpents, and harmless as doves. See clearly, speak plainly, and set no traps.

subtil.meaning: older spelling of subtle: crafty, shrewd

Noah.meaning: the man in Genesis who sent a dove from the ark

'Farthing' glossed only as a small coin; no value or conversion is claimed.
